newsitem.title: USA: U.S. zinc market stable, dealers eye LME depots.
newsitem.headline: U.S. zinc market stable, dealers eye LME depots.

text.p: U.S. zinc premiums remain steady but dealers were keeping an eye on LME stocks following a sharp hike in St Louis, while others were mystified as to who bought most of this week's Stockpile sale.

Stocks in St Louis rose some 12,000 tonnes this week and was widely said to be off-warrant material from Europe put on warrant in the Midwest location by a leading trade house who wanted to beat the June 17 introduction of amended LME rules.

From that date, each batch of zinc delivered into an LME warehouse must have a producer's certificate of analysis, or a document from an independent assayer, to assure the purity of the metal is within LME contract specifications.
"Each melt must be covered by a Certificate of Analysis and in all cases, it must be possible to cross-reference the metal to the relevant Certificate," the amended LME rules state.
Each warrant shall be made up from the production of one location and shall consist of one brand, the rules added.
Some merchants believed the metal put into St Louis is already sold, but were unsure whether more metal would be put on warrant to beat the June deadline for additional documents.
The stock hike caused barely a hiccup in zinc's steady climb on LME.

The Defense Logistics Agency also sold 7,607 tonnes of prime western and high grade zinc on Thursday, the bulk of the amount to Brown Industries, a company whose origin some traders were trying to find out.
Spot business was fairly quiet, but consumption was still good in the U.S., dealers and producers said.
"The brass and steel sectors are doing pretty well, but the alloy business is a bit slower," one producer agent said, adding that he was already sold out of material.
Zinc premiums were unchanged from last week, still at 5.00 to 5.50 cents per pound over LME cash.
